word:lxx:L700104.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “do good”: it describes carrying out an action that benefits others or accords with what is good. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it appears three times, so its basic meaning is clear even though it is not common in this corpus. The exact force of the action depends on the sentence where it occurs, but the central idea remains actively doing what is good.

word:lxx:L700148.explanation: This word means a herd: a group of animals gathered or moving together. It is a noun, so it names the animal group rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical material, it occurs ten times, showing a recurring but specific word for animals considered collectively. Its exact reference—such as the animals involved—comes from the surrounding verse, but the central meaning remains a herd.

word:lxx:L700409.explanation: This noun means “decency”: conduct marked by an appropriate sense of what is proper and respectable. It names a quality rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains decency—the quality of behaving in a fitting and respectable way.

word:lxx:L700500.explanation: Aichmalōteuō means to capture or take captive.

word:lxx:L700618.explanation: “Negate” is a verb meaning to deny, cancel, or make something ineffective. It describes an action that refuses to recognize a claim, command, decision, or effect as valid. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees, from 4 Maccabees 2:1 through 17:2. The word’s exact force in any one passage depends on what is being negated, but its central idea remains setting something aside or declaring it without effect.

word:lxx:L700654.explanation: This word is the proper name “Aleph,” also rendered “Alef.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs one time, in Joshua 19:25. The word’s specific role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here. Its lexical sense remains the name Aleph within this LXX corpus.

word:lxx:L700777.explanation: Amarphal is a proper name referring to a person named Amarphal in the Greek Old Testament. The name is preserved as “Amarphal” rather than translated into a descriptive meaning. It occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Genesis 14:1 and Genesis 14:9. Because no verse text or wider context is provided here, the name itself does not establish additional meaning beyond identifying this person. Its precise significance in either verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700823.explanation: Amiel, also rendered Amil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies individual people in the Greek Old Testament, including people mentioned in Numbers, Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The name occurs seven times in seven verses, all within the Old Testament portion of the Greek LXX. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the person being identified and the surrounding context, not from a general abstract meaning of the name.

word:lxx:L700856.explanation: Amnon is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. The name appears 35 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 29 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Samuel. It is especially prominent in the account involving David’s family, though the name itself simply identifies the person called Amnon. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700931.explanation: This word means “registering”: the act of entering or recording something in a register or written list. As a noun, it names the process rather than describing an action addressed to someone. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 2:13; the available lexical meaning is “registering.” The precise force of the noun in that passage depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L700997.explanation: Anam is a personal name, functioning as a proper noun rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:58. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, the name itself can be explained clearly, but the person’s role and significance must be determined from that passage and its wider context.

word:lxx:L701020.explanation: This verb means “dry up”: to lose moisture or become dry. It describes the action or process by which something wet or flowing becomes dry. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, across Jeremiah, Hosea, and Sirach. The word itself expresses drying rather than merely being dry, so it points to a change of condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is said to be drying up.

word:lxx:L701222.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “requite to” or “repay to,” describing an action of returning something in response to what another person has done. It functions as a verb, so it expresses the act of repaying rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 24:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the action being described.

word:lxx:L701279.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “sound in answer” or “reply.” It describes responding to what someone has said, whether by answering aloud or giving a verbal response. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 12:18. Its basic sense is therefore the act of answering or replying, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise force of that response. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

word:lxx:L701424.explanation: ἄπνοος means “without breath; lifeless.” It is an adjective describing something that has no breath or living vitality, rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it appears once, at Wisdom 15:5. That single occurrence supports a focused meaning, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what it describes there. The word’s central idea remains the absence of breath and the condition of being lifeless.

word:lxx:L701468.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means “cleanse” or “purge”: to remove what makes something unclean and bring it into a clean state. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek text of the Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 25:4. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of the word there, but its basic sense is the act of cleansing or purifying.

word:lxx:L701486.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “wash away”: to remove something by washing or by the force of flowing water. It describes an action rather than an object, so it answers what someone or something does. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 2 Chronicles 4:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the removal of something through washing or water.

word:lxx:L701675.explanation: Arabōth, also written Aravoth, is a proper name for a place. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word but as a named location in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs ten times, in passages from Numbers through 2 Kings, including references in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L701741.explanation: Ariēli, also rendered Arili, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 26:26, identifying a particular person or family name in that passage. The name itself does not provide a broader definition beyond this personal designation. Its precise significance in Numbers 26:26 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L701802.explanation: This noun refers to “rapacity” or “snatching”—taking something greedily or by force. It describes grasping behavior rather than a person or object itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages from Leviticus, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Nahum, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains forceful or greedy taking.

word:lxx:L701859.explanation: This is a proper name, identified as “Archyaioi; Arkhiei.” It refers to a named person or group rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. word:lxx:L701895.explanation: Asban, also rendered Azvan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 36:26. Its role is therefore to identify a particular person in the biblical record, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context for that occurrence.

word:lxx:L701947.explanation: This word refers to a Hasidean, or to the Hasideans as a group. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L702032.explanation: This adjective describes something that is “inconvenient” or “inexpedient”—something unsuitable, unhelpful, or not worth pursuing in a given situation. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being called unsuitable there, but the word itself carries this clear sense of what does not serve a helpful or fitting purpose.

word:lxx:L702069.explanation: This noun describes a want of discipline—disorderliness, where proper order is lacking. It refers to a condition rather than to a person, object, or specific action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 14:26. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this condition functions in that passage; the word itself supplies the general idea of disorder and lack of discipline.

word:lxx:L702234.explanation: This word means “senselessly”: it describes an action done without good sense, sound judgment, or proper consideration. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 31:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself points to behavior marked by foolishness or a lack of sensible thought.

word:lxx:L702278.explanation: Achim is a proper name, rendered as “Achim” or “Akhim.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available information establishes the name’s form and use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or his role. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical context.

word:lxx:L702371.explanation: Bazes, also rendered Vazes, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a general description or action word, but an individual name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 14:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be explained from this word alone.

word:lxx:L702465.explanation: Bakōk, also given as Vakok, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named referent rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 15:29. The name itself supplies the lexical meaning; identifying exactly whom or what it refers to requires the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L702739.explanation: This adjective describes speech or conduct that is blasphemous or defamatory—dishonoring what is holy or damaging someone’s name through insulting or slanderous words. It identifies something as offensive, abusive, or injurious in what it says about God or another person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Isaiah, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

word:lxx:L702762.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “eatage; meat”—food intended to be eaten. It refers to something used as nourishment rather than to an action or a person. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including four occurrences in Job and one in 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is food, especially meat or edible provision.

word:lxx:L702810.explanation: This adjective describes something of short performance: it is carried out briefly or does not last long. The word names the limited duration of an action or undertaking rather than expressing a person, object, or feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

word:lxx:L702933.explanation: Galgala is the name of a place.

word:lxx:L702946.explanation: Gamarias is a proper name referring to a person named Gamarias. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament text of Jeremiah, this name occurs twice, in Jeremiah 43:12 and Jeremiah 43:25. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular role in each passage must be understood from the context of those verses.

word:lxx:L703035.explanation: Gemna, also given as Yemna, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek LXX. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 15:46. Because the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific identity cannot be explained further here; its basic lexical function is simply that of a personal or place name.

word:lxx:L703127.explanation: This word means “fuller,” a noun identifying a person by that occupation. It is a specific occupational term rather than a general description of an object, action, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: in 2 Kings 18:17, Isaiah 7:3, and Isaiah 36:2. word:lxx:L703181.explanation: Gophera is a name used for a place in one passage and for a person in another.

word:lxx:L703228.explanation: Gōyni, also rendered Guni, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies an individual by name. It occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 46:24; without the verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about that person or the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is therefore its identifying name: Gōyni or Guni.

word:lxx:L703390.explanation: Deuteroō means to repeat or do something again.

word:lxx:L703512.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “testimony”—a spoken or presented witness to what is known or affirmed. It points to testimony as a declared account or statement, rather than describing the person who gives it. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, appearing once in Genesis and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains a testimony or witness-bearing statement.

word:lxx:L703549.explanation: This verb means “blow through,” describing movement through a place or opening. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Song of Songs. Its wording presents movement rather than a static object or quality: something blows through. The exact force of the image in any one verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L703585.explanation: “Diaspora” refers to a people living dispersed away from their homeland or gathered community. It is a noun naming this dispersed condition or the people who are dispersed. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs nine times, showing its use across passages about scattering and restoration. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703606.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “melt”: to become liquid or lose firmness under heat or force. It describes an action or process rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Habakkuk 3:6. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the dissolving or softening of something that was previously firm.

word:lxx:L703673.explanation: Dierchomai means to pass through. It can describe people moving through places, as David and his men did.

word:lxx:L703750.explanation: This verb means to strain off, describing the act of filtering something so that unwanted material is separated from what is being kept. It presents straining as a deliberate action rather than merely naming a strained substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 6:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is the act of straining or filtering something away.

word:lxx:L703808.explanation: This word is a proper name identifying a person, rendered “Dositheos” or “Thositheos.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it functions as a personal designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times: three times in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is intended in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L703844.explanation: Dynastes means a dynast or ruler.

word:lxx:L703893.explanation: This is a proper name, rendered in the Greek Old Testament as “Dōēk; Thik.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its ordinary function is simply to name someone. The name occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing five times in 1 Samuel and once in Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation.

word:lxx:L703945.explanation: Engyē means a pledge put into the hand: surety or security.

word:lxx:L703989.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “exercise control over.” It describes actively directing, restraining, or governing what is placed under someone’s control. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Exodus and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence identifies as being controlled.

word:lxx:L704166.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to bind something so that it hangs, or to fasten it securely. It describes attaching or securing something, with the resulting position or connection in view. In the LXX corpus, it occurs three times across Joshua, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a passage depends on what is being attached and how the sentence uses the verb.

word:lxx:L704188.explanation: This noun refers to a person who is a “searcher-out” or “inquisitor”—someone characterized by actively seeking information or examining a matter. It describes the person doing the searching, rather than the search itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Baruch 3:23. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to an investigator or questioner who pursues understanding.

word:lxx:L704247.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means “compute” or “calculate”: to work out a number, amount, or total. It describes deliberate reckoning rather than a vague estimate. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Kings. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the careful figuring or accounting of something.

word:lxx:L704302.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “break off; snap asunder.” It describes something breaking away or splitting apart suddenly, emphasizing a forceful separation rather than a gentle movement. As a verb, it expresses the action itself. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Job 18:14, so its broader range of use is not demonstrated by repeated occurrences in this corpus. The surrounding verse context would determine exactly what is described there.

word:lxx:L704359.explanation: This verb means “set on fire”: it describes causing something to catch fire or burn. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:3. Because no verse text is provided, the reference identifies its only occurrence but does not by itself show what is being set on fire or why. Its basic idea is an action that ignites something, rather than a general word for heat or brightness.

word:lxx:L704438.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “elephant,” referring to the large animal. It is used literally as a countable noun, including references to elephants in military settings and other descriptions. The word occurs five times in the LXX corpus: once in Ezekiel and four times in 1–2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the animal itself.

word:lxx:L704474.explanation: This word is the proper name “Elimelek,” functioning as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It does not provide a general concept such as a virtue, event, or physical thing; its meaning is the name itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:26. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific role there, but the word’s ordinary lexical function is simply to identify Elimelek by name.

word:lxx:L704621.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means to “spit on.” It describes the physical act of directing saliva onto a person or object. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, thing, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers and Deuteronomy, showing a specific but plainly understandable action used in those passages. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L704687.explanation: This word means “spend”. It is a verb describing the act of spending. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 23:16. The word’s basic sense remains focused and direct: it expresses spending rather than naming a person, object, or place. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but the lexical idea itself is straightforward. This occurrence belongs to the Greek rendering of the Old Testament, so it should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament term.

word:lxx:L704755.explanation: The word means “nineteen,” the number that comes after eighteen and before twenty. It is a number word, used to state a quantity rather than describe a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this entity, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 2:30. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what quantity it identifies there.

word:lxx:L704799.explanation: “Honourably” describes an action done with respect, dignity, or proper regard for another person. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Numbers 22:17. Its basic sense is therefore focused and specific: it characterizes conduct as honourable. The surrounding verse determines the precise force of that description, but the word itself presents the manner of acting as respectful and worthy of honour.

word:lxx:L705060.explanation: The verb means “bring in besides,” describing an action of bringing something or someone in along with what is already present. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 3:22. Because the word occurs only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding wording. Its central sense remains an added bringing-in.

word:lxx:L705796.explanation: Zabad, also rendered Zavath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705914.explanation: Zoob, also rendered Zoov, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705958.explanation: This proper name refers to “Ēlam” or “Ilam,” rendered in English as Elam. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears five times, in Ezra and Nehemiah. word:lxx:L706014.explanation: This word means “than.” It is used to connect one person, thing, or statement with another in a comparison, showing that one is being considered in relation to the other. word:lxx:L706137.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “marvelling”—a response of wonder or amazement. word:lxx:L706191.explanation: This verb means to “fight God”—to oppose God rather than submit to him. word:lxx:L706205.explanation: Theree is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L706292.explanation: This Greek verb means “make noise; in an uproar.” It describes noisy commotion rather than quiet or orderly activity, and it functions as an action word for becoming or being involved in such disturbance. It portrays a person whose desire for wealth has become a defining quality, rather than merely someone who owns or uses material things. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning is a covetous love of riches.

word:lxx:L713539.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “purple,” describing something marked by that color. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 1:18. The word itself identifies a visible color rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains straightforward: purple. This LXX word should be understood as a Greek rendering within the Septuagint, distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

word:lxx:L713562.explanation: This verb means to overload: to place more upon someone or something than is appropriate or manageable. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 16:33. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the act of burdening or loading someone excessively.

word:lxx:L713801.explanation: “Chelba; Khelva” is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. The two forms represent the same named individual or name rendering, rather than a general quality, action, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Judges 1:31. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide the surrounding verse text here; therefore, its particular role in that passage must be understood from the context of Judges 1:31.

word:lxx:L713980.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “gild”: to cover or decorate an object with gold. It describes an action performed on furnishings, doors, screens, and other items connected with the tabernacle and temple. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, all within eight verses, especially in Exodus and Chronicles. Its basic sense remains focused on applying gold as an outward covering or ornament, rather than simply possessing gold or making something from gold.

word:lxx:L714000.explanation: Chōma means embankment, a heap of earth.

word:lxx:L714109.explanation: Ōman, also rendered “Oman,” is a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Genesis 36:23. Because it functions as a personal or place-related name in the text, its basic meaning is its identifying designation, not a quality or concept to define. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies there.
